name: Tanning accelerator

lead: Tanning accelerators are lotions (and sometimes pills) marketed to indoor and outdoor tanners to make a tan appear faster or darker. They typically contain the amino acid tyrosine, psoralens or other chemicals, and are meant to be used together with UV exposure.

Marketing holds that tyrosine, a building block of melanin, increases pigment production; encyclopedic sources say no scientific data supports that claim. Psoralens such as 5-methoxypsoralen are photosensitizing compounds used medically in psoriasis and vitiligo, and have also been described as tanning accelerators.

paras: People apply the lotion before sun or sunbed sessions, or take pills in the run-up to tanning. A 2015 survey of 200 indoor tanners found just over half used accelerators and that users tended to tan more often.

In the 2015 survey, acne and rashes were more common among users, and adverse reactions stopped further use about 31 percent of the time. Psoralens are photosensitizers, and a rhesus monkey study found a high share of topically applied 5-methoxypsoralen was absorbed. Accelerators are used with UV exposure, a documented cause of skin cancer.

angle.text: Users apply or take tanning accelerators hoping to darken faster and deeper during UV exposure by boosting melanin production. Wikipedia notes no scientific data supports the melanin claim, and survey users report acne and rashes.

lead: Tanning accelerators are topical products, and sometimes pills, sold to speed up or deepen tanning when combined with UV exposure from sunlight or tanning beds.[1][2] The ingredients described in the literature include tyrosine, psoralens and other chemicals.[1] Wikipedia describes them as lotions or pills, usually containing tyrosine, that claim to boost melanin formation, and states that no scientific data currently supports these claims.[3]

A 2015 survey in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology reported that 53 percent of 200 indoor tanners used accelerators, that users were more likely to spray tan, tan frequently and be addicted to tanning, and that acne and rashes were more common among them.[1] The authors characterised users as high-risk indoor tanners.[1]

No clinical trials of tyrosine or similar tanning accelerators for appearance have been found. The related compound 5-methoxypsoralen has been studied pharmacologically in animals and used medically for skin disease.
infobox: No supporting scientific data per Wikipedia summary[3]

paras: Tanning accelerators are sold alongside indoor tanning lotions, often as the first lotion in a tanning routine. Some products also contain bronzers or warming agents, and patent filings describe accelerator compositions combined with bronzers.[4] Other sunless tanning products such as DHA self-tanners are a separate category that does not require UV.[3]

Psoralens appear in the sunless-tanning literature as agents that trigger melanogenesis rather than as a defined accelerator class.[3] 5-methoxypsoralen (bergapten) has been used to treat psoriasis and vitiligo and as a sun tanning accelerator.[2]

No studies found testing the effectiveness of tanning accelerators in controlled human trials. Related research includes a cross-sectional survey of 200 indoor tanners, in which accelerator use was associated with more frequent tanning, spray tanning and tanning addiction, and with acne and rashes; the authors noted that the exact ingredients were not examined and that the sample was limited.[1]

In animal work, a study in three rhesus monkeys found that after topical application of radiolabelled 5-methoxypsoralen, about 58 percent of the dose was recovered in urine, versus about 72 percent after injection, indicating high absorption through the skin.[2]
In the 2015 survey, adverse reactions to accelerators led users to stop using them 31 percent of the time.[1] Acne and rashes were more common among users than among non-users.[1]

Psoralens sensitise skin to UV light, and the monkey study's authors described the findings as part of the compound's dermatotoxic profile.[2] Dermatology literature describes UV exposure and sunbeds as major risk factors for melanoma.[1][3]
Forum discussion of accelerators is sparse in the sources reviewed, and no looksmaxxing-specific claims are documented here.
